newsitem.title: UK: Modest UK RPI masks inflation threat from services.
newsitem.headline: Modest UK RPI masks inflation threat from services.

text.p: Headline British inflation may look subdued but prices in the service sector are rising much more swiftly, suggesting an inflation threat from the largest part of the economy, economists said on Thursday.

Retail prices rose 2.6 percent in the year to June while underlying inflation held steady at 2.5 percent, bang on the government's target. But service prices were up 3.3 percent over the latest 12 months.
"We've got strong growth in services bringing a strong threat of inflation," said David Bloom, economist at HSBC James Capel.
He said James Capel had its own measure of service inflation. Unlike official data from the Office for National Statistics it excludes utilities prices which fell one percent in the year to May.
"Our measure of service inflation, excluding utilities, has it at 3.9 percent," Bloom said. "That's pretty worrying."

Britain's service sector represents about two-thirds of Britain's gross domestic product and is growing fast, buoyed by bubbling consumer spending. It also accounts for around 40 percent of the all-items RPI.
Manufacturing, hampered by the strong pound, is lagging far behind. But then again, that produces only about 25 percent of national income.
Bloom said the main reason why headline inflation figures remain subdued was the weakness in seasonal food prices, down 13.3 percent year-on-year.
Within that, the price of unprocessed potatoes are a staggering 42 percent lower than a year ago.
"It's unclear whether this is due to hot weather or the strength of the pound. But either way, the Bank will not want to rely on seasonal food prices to hit its inflation target," Bloom said.

Philip Shaw, chief economist at Union Plc, said Thursday's numbers were a little disappointing given that the pound's strength -- up about 18 percent since last August -- should be depressing import prices.
"The data also show the continued difference between subdued goods price inflation and robust prices in the service sector."

Gerard Lyons, chief economist at DKB International, agreed that service sector inflation would worry the Bank of England's new monetary policy committee even though base rates have been ratcheted up in two quarter-point notches, on May 6 and June 6.
Bloom expected rates to rise another 50 basis points to seven percent by the year-end.
"We're hoping for a budget that hits the consumer disproportionately but we're still looking for another 50 basis points on rates this year," he said.

Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown will deliver his first budget on July 2 with the skewed nature of Britain's economy crying out for personal tax rises to take the heat out of high street spending.

But not all economists forecast a burst of further rate rises. Audrey Childe-Freeman, economist at CIBC Wood Gundy, said the RPI figures, combined with the absence of pipeline pressures, would take some of the preesure off the Bank to continue tightening monetary policy.
Output prices -- those leaving the factory gate -- rose just one percent in the year to May.
But she said a clarification of the government's inflation target from Chancellor Brown would help the Bank's cause.

Brown will deliver his annual Mansion House speech to City bigwigs later. The Financial Times and two other newspapers reported on Thursday that he will introduce a symmetrical target, imposing penalties on the Bank if it misses the 2.5 percent target by 1.0 percent on either side.
Looking forward, the ONS said seasonal food prices tend to fall in June and July as do coal and solid fuel prices due to seasonal discounting.
June also traditionally sees the start of household goods and clothing and footwear sales, it said, while British Telecommunications Plc has cut certain call prices.
That will affect the June index but residential line rentals will rise on July 1, the ONS said.

Offsetting all that, housing costs will be pushed upwards after most major mortgage lenders increased their rates in response to the recent base rate rises. Rail fare increases may also come from certain companies in June, it said.
